extracted.intended_audience: Small law firms and SMMEs in South Africa (owners/agents of IPRs)
extracted.subtask_short: enforcing counterfeit goods rights South Africa
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for lodging complaints, working with inspectors and customs, collecting evidence, and pursuing criminal and/or civil enforcement against counterfeit goods in South Africa, including related advertising and consumer-protection issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterfeiting offence elements (Section 2(2) CG Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Section 2(2) of the CG Act counterfeiting is prohibited and any person found dealing in counterfeit goods is guilty of an offence if at the time of committing the act or conduct, the person knew or had reason to suspect that the goods were counterfeit goods (intent), or the person failed to take reasonable steps to avoid any act of dealing in the counterfeit goods (negligence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes both an intent and a negligence standard — prosecutions may rely on proof of knowledge/reason to suspect or failure to take reasonable steps to avoid dealing in counterfeit goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complainant eligibility for a Section 3 complaint
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person who has an interest in the protected goods, such as the owner or licensee of the IPR, importer, exporter or distributor, or their authorised agent, representative or attorney who reasonably suspects that an offence related to dealing in counterfeit goods has been, or is being committed or likely to be committed, may lodge a complaint affidavit under the CG Act with any Inspector.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complainant must have an interest in the IPR/protected goods and a reasonable suspicion; authorised agents and attorneys may lodge complaints on behalf of rights-holders.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPR evidence required in a complaint
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide evidence confirming the IPR relied upon is valid and in force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attach registration certificates or other proof showing the IPR subsists and is enforceable at the time of the complaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Details of the protected/original goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide details of the original goods where applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the genuine product sufficiently to allow comparison and identification against suspected goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particulars to show goods are prima facie counterfeit
rubrics_metrics.description: Furnish information and particulars to the satisfaction of the inspector, confirming that the goods are prima facie counterfeit goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide distinguishing features, packaging, markings, or other facts that demonstrate a prima facie case of counterfeiting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishing the offence in the complaint
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish that there is a reasonable suspicion that an offence referred to in Section 2(2) has or is being committed, or is likely to be committed, referring to the relevant act(s) of dealing in counterfeit goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set out facts showing the nature of the dealing (sale, distribution, importation, etc.) and why it meets the statutory offence elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specimen/sample of counterfeit goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a sample of the counterfeit goods or enough information to identify the distinctive features of the counterfeit goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If physical sample cannot be provided, supply detailed photographs, serial numbers, batch details or other identifiers to allow recognition and comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of infringement of the IPR
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence confirming the infringement of the trade mark, copyright works or prohibited mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attach documents, registration certificates, or other proof linking the suspect goods to the IPR and showing how the IPR is infringed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify CG Act contraventions and relief sought in complaint
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting out the provisions of the CG Act relied upon, and the relief sought in the complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly identify statutory provisions and state desired remedies (seizure, destruction, civil relief) so the inspector understands the legal basis and requested outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspector's prerequisites and powers when acting with a warrant
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the Inspector is satisfied that the complainant is entitled to lodge the complaint, that the goods are prima facie protected goods, the IPR prima facie subsists, and the suspicion upon which the complaint is based is reasonable, the Inspector must take the appropriate steps. These steps include to search, detain, and seize suspected counterfeit goods, as well as collect evidence relating to the suspected counterfeit goods or offence committed, in the appropriate manner as set out in Section 4 of the CG Act. The inspector may only act with authority of a warrant issued in terms of Section 6 and within the extent of powers outlined in Section 5(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspectors require prima facie satisfaction on entitlement, protection, subsistence and reasonable suspicion before exercising search/detention/seizure powers under warrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warrantless searches, seizures and confirmation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An inspector can, in terms of Section 5(2) search, seize and detain counterfeit goods without a warrant if there are reasonable grounds to believe that an act of dealing in counterfeit goods is being committed. Any act performed without a warrant must, in terms of Section 5(4) be confirmed by a Magistrate or Judge of the High Court within 10 working days of the date the acts were performed, failing which, all seized goods must be returned and make good any damages caused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warrantless action is permitted only on reasonable grounds and requires judicial confirmation within 10 working days; non-confirmation mandates return of goods and compensation for damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storage of seized counterfeit goods and costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon seizure, counterfeit goods are required to be stored in a counterfeit goods depot. Costs of storage are paid by the IPR owner in capacity as complainant. The goods are to remain in storage until issuance of a release notice by the Inspector, after finalising any civil or criminal proceedings against the suspect, or where an undertaking is secured from the suspect before finalising civil proceedings. Storage costs can be claimed from the suspect when instituting civil proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complainants should budget for storage costs (initially payable by IPR owner) and preserve documentation to recover costs from suspects in civil actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of a release notice
rubrics_metrics.description: The release notice: Authorises the destruction of goods (in cases where the goods have been confirmed to be counterfeit), or the return of the goods to the suspect (in cases where the time periods have not been complied with or where the goods are not found to be counterfeit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspectors issue a release notice to either permit destruction or return; ensure procedures and time-limits are complied with to avoid unintended return of goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customs brand recordal and Section 15 application (SC-CC-01-A1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Customs recordal: IPRs are protected by customs against the importation and exportation of counterfeit goods, provided the IPR owner has registered with customs for such protection. Section 15 of the CG Act allows the owner of an IPR to apply to the Commissioner for Customs and Excise (SARS) to seize and detain all goods which are counterfeit and which are imported into or enter the country. This application is called a Section 15 Application (Completed on form SC-CC-01-A1) ... Once approved, the application is valid for the period as specified in the application, up to a maximum of 10 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rights-holders should register with customs using provided form to activate border protection; approvals can be valid up to 10 years—keep filings and renewals tracked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customs border detention and sample provision procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Border measures: Customs officials may, in terms of Section 113A of the Customs and Excise Act, detain suspect counterfeit goods upon importation into South Africa. A sample of the goods is provided to the IPR owner’s appointed representatives, and a Section 3 complaint is lodged with Customs, whereafter Customs will proceed with the application for the formal seizure of the counterfeit goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate with customs and appoint representatives to receive samples promptly; follow up with a formal Section 3 complaint to trigger seizure procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seizure notice and inventory obligations (72 hours)
rubrics_metrics.description: Following the formal seizure of the goods under the CG Act, the Inspector must prepare an inventory of the seized goods within 72 hours. The Inspector must also issue the Notice of Seizure (S7(1)(d) Notice) providing details of the counterfeit goods depot where the goods will be stored, with notice to the suspect as well as the IPR owner, advising of the IPR owner’s right to lay a criminal complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspectors must act quickly to inventory and issue seizure notices; complainants should monitor timelines and ensure they receive notice to preserve enforcement options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal prosecution timelines after seizure notice
rubrics_metrics.description: If the complainant intends laying a criminal charge and request criminal investigations into the matter, this must be done within three days of issuance of the seizure notice. The State thereafter must, within 10 (working) days, inform the suspect in writing of its intention to institute a criminal prosecution for an offence of dealing in counterfeit goods, and commence criminal proceedings 10 (working) days after giving such notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complainants must act promptly (within 3 days) to request criminal investigations; be aware of the State's notification and commencement timeframes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil proceedings timelines after seizure notice
rubrics_metrics.description: If a complainant intends instituting civil proceedings against the suspect, it must provide a written notice to the suspect of its intention to bring such proceedings within 10 (working) days of the issuance of the seizure notice, and proceedings must be instituted within 10 (working) days thereafter. There is no prescribed format of the notice and usually takes the form of a letter of demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complainants should issue a written notice within 10 working days and file civil proceedings within the following 10 working days to preserve seized goods and avoid their release; keep copies of notices and proof of service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Release of seized goods where no proceedings are contemplated
rubrics_metrics.description: Seized goods to be released by the Inspector if criminal investigation or criminal or civil proceedings are not contemplated against the suspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to institute proceedings or to comply with statutory time periods will result in goods being released to the suspect — ensure statutory deadlines are met to prevent release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal penalties for dealing in counterfeit goods (Section 19 CG Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: On first conviction, a fine of up to a maximum of R5 000,00 per article, imprisonment for up to three years or both, may be imposed for each article to which the offence relates. For subsequent convictions, the maximum fine is increased to R10 000,00 per article, with a maximum period of five years’ imprisonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware penalties are per article and escalate on subsequent convictions; this can inform decisions about pursuing criminal vs civil remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain of evidence management principles
rubrics_metrics.description: To ensure that evidence is authentic and can be used in court proceedings (criminal or civil proceedings), it is critical to manage the process of tracking the movement of evidence from the time of discovery or collection until the presentation in court. The process of managing evidence is called a chain of evidence. The chain of evidence assists in proving the connection between the wrong-doer’s actions and the harm caused to you and establishing liability in civil or criminal proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep a chain of evidence record, limit the number of people handling evidence, log dates/times and handlers, properly seal or mark evidence before storage, and verify accuracy of statements and details when preparing affidavits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of evidence to collect (physical, demonstrative, documentary, testimonial)
rubrics_metrics.description: The main types of evidence collected are: Physical evidence: Physical objects or samples of infringing goods or material, usually collected through the making of a test purchase of the goods. Demonstrative evidence: photographs, diagrams, maps showing elements/locations. Documentary evidence: written or recorded documents or communications (IPR registration certificates, advertising or sales records, business documents and correspondence). Testimonial evidence: statements by persons about facts within their personal knowledge, under oath or by affidavit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use test purchases to obtain physical samples; take high-quality photographs and diagrams; collect business records showing sales/marketing; take sworn statements/affidavits from witnesses to support factual claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising Code compliance and protection of advertising goodwill
rubrics_metrics.description: The Code prohibits advertisers from taking advantage of advertising goodwill relating to the trade name, symbol of the product or service, or advertising campaign or advertising property, unless the prior written consent has been obtained from the owner of the advertising goodwill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before using another party's advertising imagery, symbols or campaign elements obtain written consent; familiarize yourself with the full Code and ensure advertising materials comply even if not an ARB member — broadcasters and many agencies are bound by the Code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative advertising limitations under the Code
rubrics_metrics.description: The Code permits factual comparisons between products and services, but with clear limitations, including: adherence to all legal requirements, including compliance with the provisions of the Trade Marks Act; claims must be capable of substantiation; claims made must not be confusing or misleading and any claim must be material, relevant and objectively determinable; and there must also be no infringement of advertising goodwill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure comparative claims are provable, non-misleading, material and legally compliant; avoid using comparative material that infringes another's advertising goodwill.

rubrics_metrics.name: ARB complaints procedure requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The ARB accepts complaints about the content of advertising. The complaint must be in writing, disclosing the identity of the complainant, setting out the grounds of complaint and relevant particulars of the advertisement, as well as the advertiser’s details, attaching relevant photographs or scan of the advertisement. Consumers can use the online complaint form (no fee); companies should try to settle disputes first and may submit a complaint via email with payment of a fee. The Directorate will consider the complaint, call on the advertiser to provide comments, attempt to resolve, rule, or refer to committee; appeals available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When lodging or preparing for an ARB complaint, gather full particulars and supporting material; be prepared to respond to the Directorate's requests and to follow appeal routes if aggrieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: ARB sanctions and remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: The ARB may order the withdrawal of the advertisement in its current format; direct the advertiser to submit a proposed amendment; require the advertiser to submit all future advertising to the ACA Advisory Service at their own cost (if repeat offender); impose adverse publicity, including publication of names of defaulters; order the defaulter to publish a summary of the ruling in media where the advertisement appeared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions range from corrective measures to reputational remedies; repeat offenders may face pre-clearance requirements and publicity sanctions — non-compliance may lead to escalation of sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: ARB jurisdiction and application to non-members
rubrics_metrics.description: The ARB is a membership-based entity, making decisions for the guidance of its members and broadcasters. Where the ARB receives a complaint against a non-member, it will give the company an opportunity to respond. If the company fails to respond or indicates that it does not regard the ARB as binding, a decision will be made simply to guide the members and broadcasters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ARB decisions primarily bind members and broadcasters; non-members may still be subject to guidance but enforcement differs — consider other statutory remedies for non-member conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambush marketing prohibition and protected events (Merchandise Marks Act Section 15A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 15A of the Merchandise Marks Act (as amended) provides that the Minister may declare certain events as 'protected events' and certain marks as 'prohibited marks' for a specified period. During the protection period, no person may use a trade mark in connection with the event in a manner intended to generate publicity or to gain special promotional benefit without prior written consent from the event organiser. 'Use of a trade mark' includes any visual or audible reproduction of the mark, as well as its use in promotional activities. Contravening these provisions is a criminal offence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not associate brands with protected events without written consent; event organisers should monitor and enforce prohibited uses during the protection window.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer rights under the Consumer Protection Act (CPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The CPA guarantees the right to fair and responsible marketing. The Act prohibits misleading advertising, unfair marketing practices and marketing that is fraudulent, false, misleading, or discriminatory. Consumer rights include: the right to equality, privacy, and freedom of choice; the right to fair and transparent disclosure of information; protection against unfair marketing practices; the right to fair, just and reasonable terms; access to goods of fair value, good quality and safety; and the right to hold suppliers accountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure advertising and product disclosures are truthful, transparent and not misleading; respect consumer rights in marketing and sales practices to avoid CPA complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplier responsibilities under the CPA
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppliers must provide accurate and transparent information, honour warranties and guarantees, resolve consumer complaints, ensure product safety, and ensure fair pricing and advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suppliers should implement compliant terms, clear warranties and complaint-handling procedures to reduce risk of enforcement by the NCC or civil claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallel imports (grey goods) legal treatment and marking requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Parallel imports are original products imported without the authorisation of the IP owner and outside the approved channel of import and supply. Trade Marks Act: importation of parallel imports does not infringe registered trade mark rights unless the goods are altered to such an extent that they are no longer original. Copyright Act: if an importer knew the import of the goods bearing the copyright work would constitute copyright infringement, this is considered copyright infringement. The CPA: Requires that parallel imports must be marked with a prominent notice advising consumers that the goods have been imported without the approval or licensee of the registered trade mark. The notice must also indicate that no guarantee or warranty will be honoured by any authorised importer of the goods. Where no such notice appears, a complaint can be lodged with the NCC (Section 25(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Importers of parallel goods must display the required prominent notice and disclaim warranties; rights-holders should monitor market and lodge complaints with NCC if marking requirements are not met.

rubrics_metrics.name: National Consumer Commission (NCC) functions and e-Service for complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: The NCC derives its powers from the CPA (Section 85). Its primary function is to enforce the CPA through consumer awareness and business guidance interventions. It handles complaints, issues and enforces compliance notices, refers anti-competitive behaviour to the Competition Commission, and refers offences to the National Prosecuting Authority. The NCC is introducing an e-Service portal that allows consumers to lodge complaints against alleged contraventions of the CPA; consumers must register and have an approved profile to lodge and track complaints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the NCC website and e-Service to lodge complaints about unmarked parallel imports or other CPA contraventions; businesses should be aware of NCC enforcement channels and compliance notices.
